en: The notation [D:
x > y] indicates that the editor, Dvivedin, [prefers reading x over y].
suggests the reading *y* instead of *x*.
In Chapter 18:
[Cb.n] indicates that the stanza is assigned the number *n* in Colebrooke’s translation.
[Cb.@] indicates that the stanza does not exist in Colebrooke’s translation.
Otherwise, the verse number coincides with Colebrooke’s.
(Colebrooke’s translation is available only for Chapters 12 and 18. In Chapter 12, all the verse numbers provided by Dvivedin coincide with those of Colebrooke.)
Since Chapter 20, concerning combinatorics related to Sanskrit prosody, has not yet been deciphered,
the text of that chapter is left exactly as it appears in Dvivedin’s edition, without the resolution of compounds or the application of sandhi rules.
[Now begins the chapter on calculation (gaṇita):
The twenty operations.
BSS 12.1a: He who understands separately the twenty operations, beginning with addition (saṅkalita), [is a true mathematician].
And he who knows the eight legal proceedings ending with the shadow becomes an expert calculator.
When the denominators of the two quantities have different divisors, they should be reduced by a common divisor;
when the denominators are equal, the numerators are to be added in the case of summation, and the difference of the numerators is to be taken in the case of subtraction.
The forms have the quality of being divisible, joined with parts, whether of two or of many;
by the division of the whole, there arises the division of the parts extracted from it.
Having transposed the divisor and the numerator of the fraction,
the denominator is multiplied by the denominator; the numerator of the dividend is multiplied by the numerator, once both have been brought to a common denominator.
The square of a fraction with a numerator and denominator multiplied by a common factor is obtained by dividing the square of the numerator by the square of the denominator;
the square root of a fraction with a numerator and denominator multiplied by a common factor is obtained by dividing the square root of the numerator by the denominator.
The last term multiplied by itself is to be set aside; it is also multiplied by three times the next term and by the first term.
The square of the next term is multiplied by the last term and by three, and the cube of the next term is added to the cube [of the first].
Subtract the square of the cube root of the second cube from three times the square of that cube root;
the result, multiplied by three times the preceding [cube root], is to be subtracted from the first cube. The cube root [of the remainder] is the [next] cube root.
In the first type [of calculation], the sum of the similar numerators and denominators, divided by the denominator, is the result;
in the second type, the numerators multiplied by the numerators and the denominators by the denominators [are the result].
In the third [result], the upper portions are multiplied by the subtrahends; in the first two, they are multiplied by the subtrahends increased or decreased by their own respective fractions.
The upper portions are [further] multiplied by the subtrahends, which have been increased or decreased by their own fractions.

In the rule of three (trairāśika), the measure (pramāṇa) and the desired quantity (icchā) are the first and last terms, while the similar quantity (sadṛśa-rāśi) is the middle term. The desired quantity multiplied by the result and divided by the measure yields the final result.
The result of the inverted triple-proportion (*vyasta-trairāśika*) is the product of the measure and the desired quantity divided by the desired quantity;
this is the result in cases of uneven triple-proportions from the first up to the eleventh.
The transference of the result from both sides should be understood as being like the destruction of a large heap [of debt] by the removal of a small [payment].
Likewise, when all [debts] are divided between both parties, there is a transference of the reduction from both sides.
In the case of exchanging goods for counter-goods, there may first be a discrepancy in value; otherwise, it is the same as what has been stated previously.
These are declared to be the refinements of the eight types of legal proceedings.
The measure multiplied by time, divided by the result, and multiplied by the difference between one and the multiplier, is the time. This,
added to its own result and divided by the sum of the root and the result, becomes the root.
The product of the time-measure and the slayer, diminished by the other time, is twofold due to the killing of the first and the mixed;
from that [value] increased by the square of half the other, the square root—diminished by half the other—is the result of the measure.
The additive factors (prakṣepaka) are the multipliers obtained by dividing [the divisor] by the quotient resulting from the subtraction of the additive; these are the gains.
When the subsequent [terms] are less or greater, the result is increased or decreased by that sum or difference, respectively. Its own fruit is then added to or subtracted from it.
In the calculation of a merchant's progression (śreḍhī-vyavahāra):

the final capital is the last term multiplied by the subsequent multiplier and added to the initial capital. The middle capital is half the sum of the initial capital and the final capital. The total sum is the middle capital multiplied by the number of terms.
In the multiplication by eight of the positive term, one should add the square of the remainder consisting of twice the subsequent term and so forth;
then, subtracting that from the square root and dividing by twice the subsequent term, one obtains the quotient.
If the sum of an arithmetic series beginning with one and increasing by one is desired,
that [sum] multiplied by twice the number of terms and divided by three is the sum of sums (saṅkalita-saṅkalita).

When that [sum] is multiplied by one, then doubled for each term, and divided by three, it becomes the sum of squares; the sum of cubes is the square of those [sums]. These are the piles formed by equal spheres.
[The calculation of the area of a quadrilateral]:
The product of the sum of the three or four sides and the sum of the opposite sides is the gross area;
the square root of the product of that sum minus twice each side is the precise area.
The difference between the squares of the two arms, divided by the earth-diameter and then subtracted from or added to the earth-diameter, and halved,
gives the respective distances (āvādha).
The square root of the square of the arm diminished by the square of its own distance gives the perpendicular (avalamba).
In the case of a quadrilateral that is neither unequal nor rectangular, the square root of the sum of the products of opposite sides is the diagonal;
the square root of the square of the diagonal diminished by the square of half the sum of the base and the top is the perpendicular.
Having subtracted the square of the hypotenuse from the square of the side, the square root is the base; having subtracted the square of the base, the square root is the altitude;
and the square root of the sum of the squares of the altitude and the base is the hypotenuse.
Alternatively, when the hypotenuse is added to the base, the resulting segments are the upper and lower portions, or they are the hypotenuse and the perpendicular.
When the hypotenuse is divided by its own square root, the two resulting products are separately multiplied by the hypotenuse and the perpendicular.
In the case of an equilateral triangle, the side is equal to twice the perpendicular dropped from a vertex;

in the case of an isosceles triangle, it is the square root of the sum of the squares of the two equal sides; and in the case of a scalene triangle, it is half the square root of the sum of the squares of the base and the difference of the other two sides.
In a triangle, the product of the two sides divided by twice the perpendicular is the heart-chord (hṛdaya-rajjū).
That [chord] doubled is the diameter of the circle touching the vertices of a quadrilateral with three equal sides.
The sum of the products of the arms as they depend on the hypotenuse should be multiplied by each other in both ways;
when divided by their sum, the results are the two hypotenuses for the case of unequal sides.
In the middle of an irregular quadrilateral, having separately conceived two irregular triangles,
one should determine the two perpendiculars and the two segments of the base by means of the two diagonals, as previously described.
In an oblique-armed triangle, having assumed the two sides as the arms and their respective perpendiculars, the upper and lower segments [of the altitude] are separately [calculated];
when added to the ears (hypotenuses), they result in the lower ears.
When divided by three, the two arms are the ground;
the perpendicular is the lower segment below the plumb-line, while the upper part is the hanging segment, which is half the sum of the plumb-lines minus the lower one.
The two segments [of the needle] are joined with the ear-hangers;
the lower parts of the ear-hangers are [determined] by proportion, while the upper parts, being deficient of those, are [determined] on the needle together with the cloth.
The square root of the sum of the squares of two unequal sides is the hypotenuse; twice the product of the two sides is the altitude;
and twice the difference of the squares of the two unequal sides is the base of the resulting isosceles triangle.
Divided by the square of the desired number, the square of the desired number is the quotient; the sum of the desired number and the quotient, halved, gives the two sides of an unequal triangle.
The sum of half the quotient and the difference between the desired number and the quotient is the base.
The square of the desired side, divided by that same desired side and then diminished by it, half of that result is the perpendicular (koṭi).
In the case of a rectangular quadrilateral, the diagonal is the square root of the sum of the squares of the two sides.
In a square where two sides are equal, the length of the ear (āyata-karṇa) is the arm (bāhu) divided by the desired [unit] and diminished by that same desired [unit];
the ground (bhū) is twice that, increased by the diagonal (koṭi); and the face (mukha) is the difference between those two.

If, after subtracting the square of the fourth side from the square of the ear (the diagonal), the remainder is greater than three times the square of the arm, it is the face; if it is less, it is the base.
In the case of four unequal sides, the two arms are the products of the two side-lengths multiplied by the opposite diagonal;
the greater [side] minus the base is one arm, and the other two arms are the remaining two sides.

The difference between the cities, multiplied by the product of the desired and the multiplier and divided by the mountain height, is the *utpāta* (elevation) for the other [city] when the two have equal motion; this result is increased by two and divided by the product of the multiplier and the multiplier.
The circumference and the area, derived from the square of the diameter and half the diameter respectively, are practical values;
when these are multiplied by ten and their square roots are taken, they yield the precise [values].
When the diameter is diminished by the arrow (śara) and multiplied by four, the square root of that product is the chord (jīvā).
The square of the chord divided by four times the arrow, increased by the arrow, is the diameter.
The square root of the difference between the squares of the two chords, divided by half the difference of the diameters, is the small arrow.
The two diameters, each diminished by the amount of the eclipse (grāsa), divided by the sum of those same diminished diameters, are the two arrows.
When the squares of the two sines (jyā-ardha) are divided by twice the desired arrow (śara), the results, added to their respective arrows, are the diameters (vyāsa).
The sum of the two arrows is the eclipse (grāsa); the difference between that sum and the diameter is the remainder of the eclipse.
The area of the excavation is the product of the field-area multiplied by the piercing-factor; this is divided by three to obtain the area of the equal excavation.
The sums of the sides equal to the face-area, divided by the number of vertices, yield the lengths of the equal cords.

The product of the area of the face and the number of facets, multiplied by the depth, is the practical calculation (vyāvahārika-gaṇita). Half the sum of the areas of the faces, multiplied by the depth, shall be the calculation according to the sūtra (autra-gaṇita).
Having subtracted the result of the calculation from the *autra* [table], one should divide the remainder by three;
having added the quotient to the result of the calculation, it becomes the precise result.
The calculation for the volume of a pile of bricks is as follows:
the area of the base multiplied by the height gives the superficial area;
this is multiplied by the height to obtain the volume; finally, dividing the volume of the pile by the volume of a single brick yields the number of bricks.
The product of the width and length in finger-breadths (aṅgulas), multiplied by the path and divided by two and four,
yields the number of cubits (kiṣkus) and finger-breadths; that is ninety-sixfold the work.
In vegetables and the like, there are two hundred; in the silk-cotton tree (*śālmali*), one hundred and twenty;
in *śāla*, *sarala*, and so forth, one hundred; and in non-wooden materials, sixty-four. [This concerns the calculation of heaps.]

The ninth [part] is for the needles, the tenth for the thick [parts], and the eleventh occurs for the fine [parts]. For the girdles, the calculation is performed by multiplying the square of one-sixth of the girdle's width.
The perimeter located at the inner and outer corners of the wall is multiplied by two, four, six, or three parts respectively.
Having performed the calculation as previously described, that result is divided by its own multiplier.
The half-day [from sunrise or sunset] divided by the shadow-man (chāyā-nara) gives the elapsed or remaining portion of the day for the east and west respectively;
the half-day divided by the degrees of the elapsed or remaining part of the day gives the shadow-man minus one.

The distance between the base of the lamp and the base of the gnomon, multiplied by the desired length of the gnomon, is divided by the height of the lamp’s flame after subtracting the gnomon’s height;
the remainder is the shadow.

The shadow multiplied by the difference between the tip of the shadow and the base is divided by the difference between the shadows; this result is the distance from the base to the lamp. That distance multiplied by the gnomon and divided by the shadow gives the height of the lamp’s flame.
The present [moment] and so forth are multiplied by the product of the qualities and the factors; the qualified [entity] is formed in the manner of a cow’s urine diagram (gomūtrikā).
Alternatively, it is added together, being equal to the difference between the qualities and the factors.
The multiplicand is multiplied by the multiplier, which is either greater or less than the desired number;
[the result] is then decreased or increased by the product of the multiplicand and the difference from the desired number, according as the multiplier is greater or less [than the desired number].
The divisor, increased or decreased by the chosen number, is divided [by the dividend]; the quotient is multiplied by the chosen number and remains undestroyed.
This is divided by the original divisor; the result, added to or subtracted from the undestroyed [divisor], is the [new] divisor.

The product of the multiplicand and the divisor, divided by the multiplier, is the quotient; the multiplier, divided by the divisor, is the multiplicand. The product of the multiplicand and the multiplier, divided by the quotient, is the divisor.
If there is a destruction of both pairs— the multipliers and the multipliers of the multipliers, as well as the divisors and the quotients obtained from those divisions—
then one should reverse those [results] and take them as desired at their respective positions.
One should multiply the multiplicand or the multiplier by the divisor of the dividend;
the divisor of the two quantities—the multiplicand and the multiplier—and the multiplier become the new divisor.
Having made the form of the divisor into the dividend, everything else is as previously stated;
or, the divisor and the multiplier should both be reduced by a common factor or multiplied by a desired number.
The square of the seconds (vikalā-varga) is obtained by multiplying the complete [minutes] by their own deficient sixtieth part and then dividing the result by thirty;
this value is to be added to the production of the complete [minutes], wherein the square and the cube are multiplied by two and three respectively.
The square of a quantity is twice that quantity minus the root, plus the square of the subtracted part;
or, it is the product of the quantity increased or decreased by an arbitrary number, plus the square of that arbitrary number.
The squares of the two desired small quantities, increased or decreased by the squares of the other deficient quantities,
are divided by twice the other quantities as increased or decreased by that [result].
That by which the divisor, increased or decreased by the result, becomes halved when added to or subtracted from the square root of the sum or difference of the squares in other positions—
or the other [value] increased or decreased by the result— is [the required quantity].
This is merely a general indication; I shall explain the rest regarding the extraction of square roots and the method of pulverization (kuṭṭaka).
In these twelve chapters on addition and the other operations, there are sixty-six verses in the Āryā meter.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the venerable *Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta*.

[Now begins the chapter on pulverization (kuṭṭaka): Since, for the most part, questions cannot be understood without the method of pulverization, I shall therefore explain the pulverization along with its problems.

The teacher [has composed this work] for those who know the *tantra* through the methods of pulverizer (*kuṭṭaka*), subtraction, addition, unknown quantities, extraction of the middle term, and problems involving a single color (*ekavarṇabhāvitaka*), as well as through the nature of squares (*vargaprakṛti*).
[The pulverizer: From the divisor of the greater remainder, divided by the divisor of the lesser remainder, take the remainder;
that which is thus mutually multiplied should be placed separately below each quotient obtained.

The remainder is likewise multiplied by the desired multiplier such that it is joined with the interval between the two remainders; the multiplier is set aside, and the quotient is multiplied by the penultimate multiplier starting from the last term.

The final denominator, joined with its own upper [numerator], becomes the numerator at the end; divided by the product of the numerators of the subtracted fractions, the remainder is multiplied by the product of the numerators of the added fractions and increased by the sum of those numerators to become the final numerator.
For the subtraction and addition of two pairs, there is the subtraction and addition of the pair-reached values of the two;
by means of pulverization (*kuṭṭākāra*), the calculation of the pair-reached values for three or more planets is performed in this manner.
The remainder starting with the *bhagaṇa* (revolutions) divided by the divisor (*cheda*), and the remainder produced by the days (*dina-ja*) divided by the same;
the first of these two, divided by the remainder produced by the days starting from the *bhagaṇa*, is the number of days (*dyu-gaṇa*).
The remainder starting from the *bhagaṇa* produced by the days, multiplied by that [quotient], results in the remainder starting from the *maṇḍala* (circumference).
The product of those two, when divided by their respective common divisors and subtracted from the quotients, yields the sequence beginning with the number of days and so forth.
When the multipliers and the divisors have been mutually divided, the remainder is used to divide those same two values;
thus, they become mutually reduced and free of common divisors.
The quotient obtained should be placed below; likewise, the remainder should be multiplied by the product of the desired multiplier.
As long as it can be subtracted, the multiplier should be placed [above], starting from the last digit, and the result should be recorded from the end.
The penultimate digit, multiplied by its own value above and added to the last digit, should then be divided.
In this manner, by means of division without remainder, the constant pulverizer (sthira-kuṭṭaka) is obtained from the remainder.
From the remainder of the desired number of lunar mansions (*bha-gaṇa*) and so forth, multiplied by the multiplier of its own pulverizer and multiplied by the divisor of its own [pulverizer],
the result is the elapsed number of days (*dyu-gaṇa*), increased by the product of the divisor and the multiplier of the subtracted *niḥpavarta*.
In this manner, when the values are equal or unequal, that which was stated regarding debt becoming wealth and wealth becoming debt—
this inversion of debt and wealth must be applied to the multiplier and the additive.
A multiplier becomes a divisor, and a divisor becomes a multiplier; a debt becomes a credit, and a credit becomes a debt.
A square root is the square, and the square is the root; the first term is the reverse of the last.
He who knows the conjunctions of the planets, as stated individually starting from the Yuga, [is a true mathematician].
He who knows the pulverizer (kuṭṭākāra) for two, three, four, and so forth, knows this.
When will the desired remainder, beginning with a lunar mansion (bha), occur on a Monday, or on a Sunday, or on a Thursday?
He who tells the signs (rāśis) [of the moon] knows the pulverizer.

When will that remainder of degrees which exists on a day of Jupiter become a remainder of minutes on a day of the Moon, or on a day of the Sun, or on a day of the Moon? He who knows this is a knower of *kuṭṭaka*. When will those desired days of the Sun and others, which exist within the measure of the lunar days (*tithis*), occur again on those same days?
He who knows the *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer) and declares [the day] on the desired planet-day is a true expert.
From the remainder of the desired number of revolutions and so forth, the number of days is determined; that is joined with the *kuṭṭaka*.
By means of those divisor-days, the day and weekday will correspond to the desired one.

He who, having observed the [mean longitudes of] the signs and so forth, calculates the number of days for a desired mean planet—whether from the conjunction of two or more planets or from the difference between two planets—is a knower of the pulverizer (*kuṭṭaka*). [BSS 18.20] [The result is obtained] by multiplying the divisor of the remainder by the [longitude in] signs and so forth, including the minutes and so forth, and then dividing [the product]. [BSS 18.21]

The remainder of the revolution (maṇḍala-śeṣa) obtained by dividing by the *bhagaṇa* units is the number of days (*ahargaṇa*). In this same manner, from the remainders of signs, degrees, minutes, and seconds, the number of days is found as before. When the values are lost, one should take those desired quantities, divide them as stated, and [retain] the remainder.

He who, being an expert in *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer), calculates from the stated remainders of signs, degrees, minutes, and seconds those desired lost quantities along with their intermediate values— he is a knower of *kuṭṭaka*. That by which the multiplier, increased by the remainder, is divisible when divided by its own multiplier and subtracted from the divisor— [that is the pulverizer].

The remainder of that [product] is the fruit; likewise, from the remainder, one obtains the number of days and planets. He who knows the elapsed yuga from the stated remainder of intercalary months (*adhimāsa*), or from the remainder of omitted lunar days (*avama*), or from their sum, is a knower of *kuṭṭaka*.
On the days of the desired measurement, or when there remains an intercalary month or deficient nights,
he who further declares these either individually or separately is a knower of *kuṭṭaka*.
From the remainder of the degrees diminished by three and divided by seven, the square root is diminished by eight.
When will nine hundred and ninety-nine, increased by its own form (i.e., 1000) and multiplied by nine, equal the number of days of the sun on a Wednesday?
The square root of the remainder of the deficient months after subtracting three, increased by two and divided by six— when will that square, decreased by two and increased by nine, become ninety?
When does the group of the remainder of the least, increased by two, divided by twenty-one, multiplied by eight, divided by ten, and increased by two, equal eighteen? [The result is zero,
representing neither wealth nor debt.]
The sum of two positive quantities is positive; the difference between two negative quantities is negative; the difference between a positive and a negative quantity is their sum;

and the sum of a positive and a negative quantity is their difference. Zero added to or subtracted from a positive or negative quantity remains that same quantity; and zero added to or subtracted from zero remains zero. A smaller number is to be subtracted from a larger one; a positive quantity is subtracted from a positive, and a negative quantity is subtracted from a negative.
The difference between those two may be either negative or positive; a debt becomes a credit, and a credit becomes a debt.
A debt diminished by zero remains a debt, while a credit diminished by zero becomes zero, which is space.
When that which is to be subtracted is a credit from a debt, or a debt from a credit, then it should be added.
The product of a debt and a wealth is a wealth; the product of two debts is a wealth; and the product of a debt and a wealth is a debt.
The product of zero and a debt, or of a wealth and zero, or of two zeros, is zero.
A wealth divided by a wealth is a wealth; a debt divided by a debt is a wealth; and zero divided by zero is zero.

Food is subtracted from debt; wealth is subtracted from debt; debt is subtracted from wealth; thus, debt becomes debt. (BSS 18.34c) A debt or wealth that has been subtracted from zero, or divided by that same zero, or divided by the product of debt and wealth, results in zero. (BSS 18.35a) The square of a debt or of wealth is positive; the square root of zero is zero; and the square of that [zero] is [again] zero. (BSS 18.35c)
[The Transition] The yoga, increased or decreased by the interval and divided by two, is the transition; or else,
the square of the interval, increased or decreased by the interval and divided by two, is the uneven operation.
The *karaṇī* is the hypotenuse;
its square, divided by the chosen number (*iṣṭa*), when decreased or increased by that same chosen number, yields the smaller and larger sides respectively.
The larger side, divided by two, is the base (*bhuja*). The product of these two is the square of the area.

The square of the sum of the desired subtracted *karaṇī* roots, multiplied by the desired number, or the square of their difference; this is the multiplicand placed horizontally, with the multiplier repeated below it, and the product of these added together. [Cb.39]
The dividend and divisor, joined separately and repeatedly with the square of the desired number and the subtraction of the debt,
are such that the dividend— divided by the divisor located in one place— is either a square or twice the product of two equal numbers. Alternatively,

when the square of the unit (rūpa) is diminished by the desired surd (karaṇī), the half of the difference between the square root of that result plus the unit and the square root minus the unit [is the desired surd].
First, the square; then another, the second, which is the root repeatedly extracted.

[BSS 18.40c] The addition and subtraction of like quantities—such as the square of the unmanifest (the unknown), the cube, the square of the cube, the fifth power, the sixth power, and so forth—and of unlike quantities separately. [BSS 18.41a–c]
The square of two like [terms] is one class; the product of three and so forth is another class belonging to that; the product of different classes is yet another.
The multiplication of the various classes is to be performed as before; the remainder is as previously described.
[End of the section on the reduction of like terms.]
When the square roots of the unknowns (*avyakta*) are subtracted from each other, the remaining distinct forms are equal;
the unknowns (*avyakta*) are to be subtracted from those forms which stand below them.
[Cb.44] When the squares of the forms multiplied by four are combined with the middle square, [the process continues].
The square root of twice the square of the middle term, diminished by the product of the first term, is the middle term.
Of the squares multiplied by the coefficients and increased by the square of half the unknown,
the square root diminished by half the unknown and divided by the coefficient is the unknown.
When the remainder of the twelfth part of that which remains after subtracting one part is four times itself plus eight,
and equal to that same remainder of one part, then tell me the number of elapsed days.
The remainder of the omitted months, diminished by two, divided by three, increased by seven, and multiplied by two—

When the remainder of the intercalary months is equal to that [value], then state the elapsed portion of the yuga. (BSS 18.47c) When the remainder of the omitted lunar days (*avama*), divided by six, increased by three, is equal to the remainder of the omitted lunar days divided by five, then state the elapsed portion of the yuga. (BSS 18.48a–c)
When the square root of the remainder from the mandala— reduced by two, multiplied by ten, increased by two, and further reduced by one—
is equal to the remainder from the mandala reduced by one, on what day of Mercury does this occur for the Sun?
When is the square of the remainder of the intercalary months, diminished by three, equal to that remainder of the intercalary months?
Or, when is it equal to the remainder of the omitted lunar days (*avamāvaśeṣa*) derived from the remainder of the omitted lunar days?
[This is the solution for equations involving multiple unknowns.]
Subtracting the other denominators from the first denominator, and dividing the first numerator by the first denominator;
repeating this process until the subtrahends are equal, the two resulting values, when subtracted from each other, yield the results for many cases through the *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer) method.
[From the number of days elapsed] added to the completed revolutions, and [from that same number of days] added to its remainder, and [from that] combined with their sum—

He who, knowing the *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer), declares the number of days from that conjunction, is a master of the pulverizer. He who, knowing the *kuṭṭaka*, declares the number of days from the number of elapsed revolutions subtracted [from the current day], or from the remainder thereof subtracted [from the current day], or from the difference between those two subtracted from their sum, is a master of the pulverizer.
The one who, by means of the remainders of those [divisors] starting with the zodiacal sign (*rāśi*), diminished by the elapsed days and intercalary months,
and likewise by their respective remainders, declares the elapsed *yuga*, is a knower of *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer). Alternatively,
from the remainder of the minutes (*liptā*) increased by the remainder of the degrees (*aṃśaka*), or from the difference between them, [the elapsed time is determined].
The knower of *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer) who declares the number of days for the Sun on a Wednesday—[that is the one].
When will the remainder of the degrees of the Sun on a Wednesday be three, and the remainder of the minutes six, seven, eight, or nine? Let the calculator determine this within the course of a year.

On the desired day, up until the end of the year, the calculator should determine the remainder of the *aṃśas* as equal to the *aṃśas*, or the remainder of the *kalās* as equal to the *kalās* of the sun; likewise,
he should determine the remainder of the *avamas* by means of *avamas*, and the remainder of the intercalary months (*adhimāsaka*) by means of intercalary months.
The calculator, performing the addition or subtraction of the desired [corrections] until the year is reached, [obtains the result].

(BSS 18.58c) The divisor and multiplier for the sun are zero; the quotient, diminished by the remainder of the degrees and multiplied by seventy, is divided by ten thousand; the calculator performs this until the year is reached. (BSS 18.59a–c)
The multiplication of the modified form by its own unmodified divisor, divided by the desired divisor, yields the two desired quotients.
When the smaller is greater and the greater is smaller, the difference should be added; when the modified quantity is subtracted, the process is reversed.
Having subtracted from the product of the signs and degrees of the Sun (multiplied by three and four respectively) the signs and degrees [of the Moon],
and having observed ninety [degrees], the calculator makes the Sun [complete] within the year.
In the hypothetical case, the products are equal in measure to those [quantities] whose unknowns have been eliminated.

Having performed the operations, the unity of the affected color becomes the [resulting] figures. Thus, the product of the measure of the color multiplied by the affected quantity becomes the number of the desired color.
This is established even without the operation of equalizing the affected quantities; what, then, has been achieved by that?
The square-root is twofold: from the square of the *iṣṭa* (the chosen number) multiplied by the multiplier, and from that same square increased or decreased by the *iṣṭa*.
The product of the first [root] multiplied by the multiplier, together with the product of the last [root], constitutes the final [root].
The first [root] is the square root of the product of the original [number] and the augment, equal to the product of the augment;
when divided by the subtractive augment, the roots are obtained with the augment as the constant term.
When the roots are separately increased or decreased by the desired augment and the constant term, [the results are the other roots].
Having performed the addition or subtraction of desired values in the last and first terms, [the following applies]:
When four is added, the square of the last term diminished by three, halved, and multiplied by the last term, yields the last term.
The square of the last term minus one, divided by two, and multiplied by the first term, yields the first term.
In the case of a square diminished by four, subtract three and one from the square of the last term; let the resulting half be separate and increased by one.
Multiply this by the first term plus one, and multiply the first term by the product of the last term and the first term.
When the multiplier is a square, the additive is divided by some number, then added to or subtracted from it, and halved.
The first [root] is the square root of the last term; the other [root] is obtained by dividing the product of the coefficients by that first root.
When the multiplier is divided by a perfect square, the first [root] is divided by the square root of that [square];
when the additive is divided by a perfect square, the roots are then multiplied by the square root of that [square].

The sum of the multipliers multiplied by eight and divided by the square of the difference between the multipliers is the quantity (*rāśi*). When the two multipliers are tripled and subtracted in reverse order, they are divided by their difference to yield the two square roots (*pade*). A square, increased or decreased by another square, when divided by the square of half the sum or difference of those two, [yields the other root].

The sum and the difference of those two, multiplied by that [number], and their squares, plus one, are the products. By those amounts subtracted from and added to the square, their sum divided by an arbitrary number (iṣṭa), and the square of half that [quotient] minus the arbitrary number, results in a quantity that is either less or greater; this is the value of the original term.
The difference between those two quantities by which the square is greater or less is divided by or subtracted from the desired number;
the square of that result, increased or decreased by the same amount, yields the two quantities—the greater and the lesser—for the case where the square is greater or less.
[Examples]
The astronomer, performing the square of the remainder of the signs and degrees— multiplied by ninety-two or multiplied by eighty-three,
plus one— on a Wednesday, [continues] until the end of the year. Likewise, the remainder of the solar seconds is multiplied by five less than ten (i.e., five).
A calculator, performing the square of the remainder of the revolutions of the asterisms (bhagaṇa) and so forth on a Thursday, for up to a year; or adding three times that square to nine hundred,
or subtracting eight hundred from the square, for up to a year— [such a person] is a calculator.
The calculator, performing the square of the remainder of the desired revolutions and so forth— multiplied by four and added to sixty-five,
or subtracted from sixty— until the end of the year;
[then] the remainder of the desired revolutions and so forth, multiplied by eighty-three and subtracted by ninety-two.

The calculator, performing the squaring of the remainder of the intercalary months, multiplies it by thirteen, adds three hundred, and subtracts the cube of three, continuing this squaring process for up to a year. (BSS 18.80) The calculator, forming a square sum endowed with its form, continues this for up to a year. (BSS 18.79)
The calculator, multiplying the remainder from the moon by seventeen and also by thirteen,
adds one to each separately and squares them until the end of the year.
He then multiplies the square of the remainder from the omitted days (*avama*) by twelve and adds one hundred.
Subtracting three from the square until the year is reached, the calculator [performs this];
on the day of Mercury, the remainder of the sun’s minutes is increased by the remainder of Jupiter’s seconds and then subtracted;
performing the square and the multiplication plus one until the year is reached, the calculator [proceeds].
An astrologer, while calculating the square of the Sun on a Wednesday up to the end of the year, [uses] the remainder of the degrees as ninety-three less sixty-seven.
On a Wednesday, the remainder of the Sun's minutes is increased by twelve and sixty-three.
Subtracting sixty and eight [degrees] until the end of the year, the calculator [determines the result];
from the remainder of the minutes of the moon, the remainder of the minutes of the sun, or the remainder of the degrees,
or else performing the desired mean [calculation] until the end of the year, the calculator [proceeds].
The astronomer, calculating Jupiter from the remainder of the *jīva* [sine] of the moon, Mars from the remainder of the *bhūmi-liptās*,

and the Sun from the remainder of the lunar degrees, [obtains the results] up to the end of the year. From the desired planet and its respective remainder, the day-count (*dyu-gaṇa*) is obtained by multiplying it with the elapsed days multiplied by the divisor.
If the remainder of another planet’s calculation is greater than this by subtraction or addition, it is desired; otherwise,
the subtraction and division of the days for the two planets are reversed from the total number of days.
Because, by subtracting that [value] from both [the quantities], the two extracted [roots] are multiplied together.
The subtraction and addition of the parts are reversed; from that sum again,
in the case of the remainder, one proceeds from the day-count (*dyugaṇa*) for three and so forth on the desired day, as previously described.

The sun and moon, whether in their mean or their true positions, are derived from the remainder of the omitted days (*avama*) multiplied by the number of days elapsed; thus the calculator produces the lunar day (*tithi*) or the planet up to the end of the year. When the remainder of the omitted days for a single day is multiplied by a certain factor and diminished by the number of revolutions of one sun, one moon, or a planet, [the result is the respective true position].
It is purified by the quotient of the remainder of omitted days (*avamāvaśeṣa*) divided by earth-days (one thousand five hundred and twenty-one); this is the statement regarding the lunar months.
From the remainder of omitted days multiplied by arrows (five), arrows (five), arts (sixty-four), and directions (ten)—that is, by 10,845—[the result is] the number of days;
the remainder is obtained by dividing by form (one), eight, Vedas (four), flavors (six), zero, and arrows (five)—that is, by 3,506,481.
From the remainder of the omitted days (*avamāvaśeṣa*), that which remains is the remainder of the solar revolutions (*ravibhagaṇa*).
(BSS 18.94c) [This remainder] is multiplied by 110,179 and divided by 3,562,220.
(BSS 18.95a) The remainder from this is the *tithis* from the remainder of the omitted days; the remainder from the omitted days itself is the *vikala*. (BSS 18.95c)
Having observed the sum of the degrees, minutes, and seconds, as well as the difference in seconds, what remains?
The sum is divided in two ways—once by the excess and once by the deficiency—and the results are halved to obtain the two remainders.
The difference between the squares of those two remainders is the first remainder; that difference, when added to or subtracted from the previously obtained difference, is the second remainder.
The difference between the squares is divided by two; the remainder from that is the day-count (dyugaṇa).
Having subtracted the square of the sum from twice the product of the roots, the square root of the remainder is taken.
That [root] added to and subtracted from the sum, halved, yields the two desired remainders separately.
From the square of the remainder multiplied by two, increased by the square of the difference between the remainders, one takes the square root;
this, when decreased by or added to the difference between the remainders and halved, yields the values for the two desired remainders separately.
These problems involve multiplication by the heart (the multiplier); one may construct thousands of other such problems from them.
Having stated the questions given by others, one should resolve them by means of these calculations;
in the assembly of people, he destroys the brilliance of those who know fate, just as the sun destroys the light of stars.
What need is there to mention even those recited as problems on pulverizers (*kuṭṭākāra*) by the hundreds?
In each of these sūtras, along with their respective headings, these questions have been recited;
and by means of one hundred and three Āryā verses, eighteen chapters on pulverization (kuṭṭaka) have been completed.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, on the *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer), in the illustrious *Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta*.
[Knowledge of the gnomon-shadow and so forth] [Questions]:
Having observed the ghaṭikās of midday, he who knows the sun understands the degrees of latitude (akṣāṃśaka).
The knower of the system should determine the unknown from the known by means of the ghaṭikās between two risings.
He who, from the known [mean longitude], brings forth the unknown by means of eight intervening ghaṭikās,
and from that calculates the mean motion and the revolutions of the asterisms for a yuga— he is therefore a knower of the treatise (tantra).

The knower of the system (tantra) who understands the measurement of the shadows on the ground between the base of the gnomon and its tip can determine the measures of the sun and moon from the height of the lamp-flame.

One who knows the height of the desired house and knows the distance between it, when looking at it in water, or [at its reflection] in a mirror, shows the top of the house wall; he is a knower of the *tantra*.
By knowing the difference between the length of the shadow and the second part of the base, one understands the height of a lamp;
or, by knowing the shadow of a gnomon, the knower of the system understands the shadow of the earth.
Having seen [the sun] through the lattice-windows on the upper floor of the house, and having seen the top of the house, one who knows the ground [determines the direction]. [Alternatively:
having seen it in the water between the people of the house.]
Or, having seen [his reflection] in oil, one who knows the treatises perceives the height of his house.
Having observed the top of the house and then extending his gaze into the water,
one who knows the system (*tantra*) brings the ground from the water back to the knowledge of his own site, or determines the height of the house.

He who understands how the reflection of the sun’s light ascends upon a wall— when the shadow-persons are known by those who know, and when the opening between water and a wall is discerned— is a knower of the *tantra*.
The half-ghaṭikās from the desired day, the breaths at intervals of fifteen ghaṭikās,
and the breaths of the diurnal motion for that day— one should calculate the axle with these as before.
The difference between the rising times of the known planet and the known longitude of the object sought is greater or less than the nāḍīs [of the interval];
the object sought is known from the known planet by means of the rising times, whether it precedes or follows it.
The known half-asterism (bhārdha), increased or decreased by the rising and setting intervals in nāḍīs, is to be understood as being before or after the known [half-asterism];
it is to be known when the known [half-asterism] is deficient by one half-asterism.
Having established the middle [longitude] as known, the daily motion for the following day is determined from that interval;
by means of the rule of three (trairāśika) applied to the motion, the calculation of the planetary mandala for a kalpa is obtained.
The magnitude of darkness (tamas) during an eclipse is clearly the reverse of half the duration;
it is measured from the rising of the Sun or Moon until the end of the portion of the lunar mansion (bha).

The distance between the base of the lamp and the base of the gnomon, multiplied by the desired length of the gnomon, is divided by the height of the lamp-flame minus the height of the gnomon; the result is the shadow.

The shadow multiplied by the distance between two gnomons and divided by the difference between the shadows is the height of the ground. The same height, multiplied by the gnomon and divided by the shadow, is the height of the lamp.
Having determined the shadow of the gnomon, one should calculate the heights [of objects] through proportion;
or, having ascertained the height of a house, a shrine, a tree, or a mountain, one may determine the shadow.
The difference in degrees, multiplied by the height of the aspect, is indeed divided by the house-height and the height of the aspect.
When water is poured, the best omen for the house is the appearance of a fruit upon it.

Having observed the top of the house through the water at a distance from the house, the height [of the house] is obtained by multiplying the height of the observer's eye by the distance between the house and the water,
and dividing by the distance between the person and the water.
The distance from the water to the top of the submerged object, when subtracted from the sum of the first and second [measures], is the height of the water above ground.
The height of the object above the water is the product of the height of the observer's eye and the distance between the man and the water, divided by the difference between those two distances.
The shadow-man, the severed [object], and the attainment of the interior of water or a wall through ascension;
this nineteenth chapter of the twenty Āryā verses is concluded.
[Regarding the *chandas-citi* section:
A group of verses (*ṛgvarga*) constitutes a cycle (*paryāya*) in the *samūha*, *yoga*, and *avayuk* types, as well as in the *yugma* type.
In the *soya* type, as previously established, there are groups of four; the final one is determined by the remaining method.

In the case of the squares and other powers, one should increase the quarters (pādas) in direct and reverse order for those with odd indices, starting from one and alternating by adding or subtracting until the end is reached; this process is the reverse of that [for even indices].
By adding one to each [number] up to two, three, and so on, among those established upon that [base], the *prastāra*—
beginning with the class (*varga*) and ending with the desired [term]— becomes "middle-like-barley" (*yavamadhya*).

The final number of the sequence is divided by two; for the numbers beginning with three, the individual counts below it are subtracted from that [final number] minus one, and the resulting forms are added individually to those above.
As long as one proceeds by adding one to the digits, starting from the units place,
the highest number among those beginning with the square root and so forth is obtained by multiplying the product of the digits starting with the units by the square and so on.
In the uneven [feet], the upward [measure] is one and a half times the measure of the syllables; in the even [feet], it is twice the measure of the syllables.
Below that, for all [the feet], there are two, one, and zero units.
With middle [syllables] that are likewise reduced by half, there are those beginning with a dissimilar foot equal to the first;
having displaced one from the middle of the uneven [pādas], one should place it elsewhere at the beginning.
The arrangement [of the numbers] is increased by one, equal, and so forth, and subtracted below;
the sum of the numbers is such that it remains the same as the first when three are removed upon the loss [of a term].
When the number is even, the products formed by the middle terms and those by the halves, being equal in number, are to be added in direct and reverse order;
when the number is odd, one is subtracted, and the half is added in direct and reverse order along with one.
In the case of equal numbers, [the sequence] should be constructed through ascending and descending orders of steps, and likewise through unequal ones;
when the first [term] is seen in the calculated result, the remaining syllables are at the end.

In the case of equal, deficient, equal-and-deficient, and unequal [coefficients], there is the elimination of the number of terms, half the terms, and all terms respectively. By other terms, there is the elimination of the leading term; by those same terms plus one, there is the elimination of both the self-term and the other-term, as previously described.
The one immediately following the first is the *adhahkalpa*; the first is equal to the others before it;
the *nyāsa* is the square; and the *prastāra* belongs to the half-even and uneven meters.
When subtracted from the elapsed [period], the product of the lower number of kalpas is divided by the sum of the odd numbers;
[the result] minus one, when separately divided by its own square root, yields the result for the equal kalpas.
When the number of past [terms] is indicated and subtracted from the total, the first result is the same as the original; otherwise, it is different.
When the square roots are repeatedly added together, one is added, and then halved, for both even and odd numbers.
In the case of the *kapi* (monkey) permutations, the number of heavy and light syllables is divided individually by one and so forth, as before.
In the case of odd numbers, the *meru* diagram for those starting with even numbers is obtained by subtracting the initial light syllables from the total number of light syllables.
Beyond one and two, the sequence below is doubled from the immediate predecessor and differs in form;
starting from the square-root holder, the flag-sign (dhvaja) occurs for the even and odd positions of the roots of the squares by means of the light syllables.
When the number of light syllables is divided by the feet and then purified by successive divisions from below,
using pure numbers ending in two and followed by squares, the *mandara* meter is formed by those light syllables.
Having arranged below each [number] the figures one and so on, increasing by one in succession,
the sum of the others from its own position downward is obtained here as before, starting from the first, according to the method of the array.
The number [of finger-breadths] shall be double the six ghaṭīs of the Guru;
this is the twenty-second chapter on the meters of the Āryas, concerning the construction of the funeral pyre.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, on the determination of the meters, in the venerable *Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta*.

[The Chapter on the Bowstring] BSS_21.17a: Having marked the numbers at the eighth parts of the radius, proceeding in order and reverse from the joints of the feet, BSS_21.17c: one should fasten strings between each pair; these are the bowstrings, and their halves are the half-bowstrings.
The segments of the sines (jyākhaṇḍas) are the intervals between the half-sines;
these are subtracted from the last one, and then the arrow (iṣu), the versed sine (utkramajyā), and the arc (dhanus) are derived from those two.
From the square roots of one-fourth of the squares of the semi-diameters increased by one, two, and three units respectively,
there arise other segments of eight, twelve, and sixteen parts.

Having subtracted from the square of half the base (vyāsa-ardha) one-fourth of the sum of the squares of the equal segments of the chords corresponding to the equal and reverse orders, the first root is obtained as that which remains undestroyed.
The fragments of those petals are equal to the Jinas diminished by that [number]; this is the second [set] at the time of origination.
[The sequence begins with] two, Yamala, one, direction, lord, arrow, seven, taste, quality, nine, and so forth.
In this manner, the segments of the chord (jīvā-khaṇḍas) are either few or many, beginning with the first segment;
these are the half-chords corresponding to the sixth, fourth, and third parts of the circumference of the circle.
Alternatively, by multiplying the diameter by the difference of the squares of the [successive] increments, or by taking one-fourth of that,
and having performed the aforementioned operations for the segments, the calculation of the half-chord is not simplified thereby.
